newsitem.title: russia: Chechen poll frontrunner demands sovereignty.
newsitem.headline: Chechen poll frontrunner demands sovereignty.

text.p: The former guerrilla commander who is widely expected to win Chechnya's presidential election vowed on Sunday to turn Russia's rebel region into an internationally-recognised sovereign state.

Aslan Maskhadov, speaking to reporters near the Chechen capital on the eve of the election, also said that as president he would seek "war reparations" from Russia to compensate for the devastation caused by 21 months of fighting.

He dismissed fears of an "Afghan or Tajik scenario" of civil war as a product of the rhetoric of hardline rivals such as Shamil Basayev. Victory for Basayev, who once led a bloody raid on a Russian town, could fulfil Moscow's worst nightmares.

Basayev aides said their candidate had little hope of winning an outright victory but aimed instead to come in second, holding Maskhadov to less than 50 percent of the vote and thereby forcing a second round of voting in two weeks time.

"We hope to get between 30 and 32 percent," said an aide at Basayev's noisy Grozny headqurters."If there is a second round then we can beat Maskhadov, because all of the other candidates will back us." That prediction seems rather unlikely.

Basayev has gone to his home in the mountainous Vedeno region of southern Chechnya, but former fighters milled around the brick two-storey headquarters. Some drank tea and watched videotaped action clips from the war.

Sixteen candidates initially stood for president, but only Maskhadov, Basayev, acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov are serious contenders. Three minor candidates pulled out on Sunday.
Maskhadov, 45, said Moscow seemed in no mood to negotiate giving Chechnya's de facto independence more legal substance, but he added: "We want to be recognised as a sovereign state."

"The whole world, including Russia, will have to recognise that the elections are democratic and to recognise the legitimate authority of this popularly-elected president and sit down at the negotiating table right away," he said.

In Moscow, Deputy Foreign Minister Viktor Posuvalyuk underlined Kremlin sensitivity over the sovereignty issue, saying Russia was ready to break relations with any country which recognised the north Caucasus region.
"We have warned the entire international community," he said, but acknowledged there was no sign yet of any country making a move to do so.

President Boris Yeltsin sent troops into Chechnya in 1994 to prevent it seceding but failed to subdue Maskhadov's fighters. For Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery and pneumonia, the mere holding of the elections constitutes a defeat.
But few countries would entertain the notion of sacrificing relations with Russia in order to recognise a region with a prewar population of just one million people.

The Chechen authorities have laid on tight security for more than 100 outside observers, including Russians, who have arrived to monitor the election. Armed police patrolled snowy Grozny, warming their hands over bonfires.

The chief European mediator in Chechnya, Tim Guldimann, said the 75 monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe would have armed Chechen escorts and helicopter cover and would be in constant radio contact.
"I don't see any problems with these elections from the security point of view," the Swiss diplomat told Reuters.
Chechnya is awash with guns, however, and the increasingly bellicose rhetoric of the election campaign has kindled fears that factional fighting could erupt.

Basayev, popular among the young, espouses a fervent brand of Islamic rule. He could force a run-off, as might Yandarbiyev, who became the rebels' leader when Dzhokhar Dudayev was killed last April. Udugov also has solid support.

In their first internationally-monitored elections, Chechens will also choose from among some 850 candidates standing for 63 seats in a new regional assembly. First results are expected late on Monday or early on Tuesday.
